title: Active Budget Allocation for Efficient Scaling Law Estimation via Surrogate-Guided Pruning
claim: Uniform and halving-only allocation pick a worse candidate; adding a surrogate predictor selects a better one and reaches lower final loss.
layout: 3 panels, left-to-right, shared axes, red selected curve, × minimum marker
description: Three side-by-side line plots share a log-scale loss axis, with 10^1 at the top. Each plot shows about six green learning curves that fall from upper left to lower right. Smaller models sit to the left and plateau earlier. One curve in each panel is red, marking the model chosen for final-round training. A black × at the end of the red curve marks the minimum loss. Legend boxes give the final loss for each strategy: L=3.46 for uniform allocation, 3.15 for successive halving, and 3.09 for successive halving with a surrogate. The × sits lower in each panel from left to right. The red curve differs in the right panel, where the surrogate picks a more promising model. The eye goes first to the red curve and the × marker, then to the legend numbers.
caption: Comparison of different compute budget allocation strategies using the synthetic LC dataset. Approaches are described in Section 3. Left: Conventional uniform allocation. Middle: Successive Halving (SH). Right: Successive Halving with multitask Gaussian Process (LMC) surrogate model. Green curves denote observed learning curves for models of different sizes, where smaller models appear to the left and plateau earlier. The red curves indicate the model selected for further training in the final round. SH-LMC uses its surrogate prediction to select a different and ultimately more promising model than plain SH, achieving a lower minimum loss (marked by ×).
abstract: Predicting model performance at larger scales enables the design of training strategies and architectures tailored to specific performance targets. Empirical scaling law research identifies functional forms to aid this prediction task. These describe the relationship between loss and compute using a loss-compute frontier defined by learning curves. Due to the empirical nature of this approach, the computational burden is substantial, making strategic resource allocation essential - yet it remains surprisingly underexplored. In this work, we address this shortcoming by exploring the suitability of Successive Halving (SH) and SH combined with parametric and non-parametric surrogate models. In addition to enabling a more systematic allocation of a given compute budget, our findings show that SH paired with surrogate models yields a set of learning curves that includes one with a lower loss-compute value than what naive uniform allocation or an SH-only approach can obtain. Our experiments demonstrate mean relative improvements of up to 2.84% and 5.47% on real-world and synthetic learning curve datasets. This strategic resource allocation enables us to obtain accurate scaling laws at significantly reduced computational costs, saving up to 98.7% over the traditional exhaustive approach.
